guide.title: Unit 2 study guide
guide.headline: Networks of Exchange. Connect the routes.
guide.essential: How did networks of exchange change economies, states, cultures, and environments from c. 1200 to c. 1450?
guide.overview: Between c. 1200 and c. 1450, older Afro-Eurasian exchange networks intensified without becoming one unified system. Demand for luxury and everyday goods encouraged production, while caravan services, credit, ports, ships, camel logistics, and state policy changed what movement was practical. The Mongol Empire connected large overland regions through conquest and administration, yet local experiences ranged from facilitated travel to destruction and coercion. Indian Ocean sailors used seasonal winds and maritime technology, and port communities turned repeated voyages into diasporas and cultural adaptation. Trans-Saharan routes linked desert logistics to West African production, taxation, pilgrimage, and scholarship. Connectivity moved crops, knowledge, religions, people, animals, and pathogens. Those consequences were uneven: a crop could widen food possibilities while disease or intensified land use created serious costs. The unit’s networks overlapped, and the most defensible arguments explain both shared pressures and differences in geography, power, and community agency.

timeline.text: Older Silk Roads, Indian Ocean routes, Saharan crossings, farming systems, and religious networks created the foundations later intensified.
Temüjin was recognized as Chinggis Khan, beginning the political consolidation that launched Mongol expansion.
Mali expanded in West Africa; the Delhi Sultanate began in 1206; Mongol conquests reshaped Eurasian politics and routes.
The Mongols captured Baghdad. Political change did not end Islamic scholarship or cultural exchange across the region.
The Mongol Yuan dynasty completed the conquest of the Southern Song, bringing China under Mongol rule.
Mansa Musa made a pilgrimage to Mecca that displayed Mali’s wealth and strengthened its wider Islamic connections.
Bubonic plague spread through connected regions, causing severe and uneven demographic consequences.
The Ming replaced the Yuan in China, illustrating political change within the same wider exchange era before the later Zheng He expeditions.
Zheng He led Ming maritime expeditions across the Indian Ocean as state-sponsored diplomacy and display.
The unit ends before the major European maritime expansion of the later fifteenth century; later developments are context, not Unit 2 evidence.

pitfalls: The Silk Roads were a connected set of routes, not one uninterrupted road traveled by every merchant.
Mongol political fragmentation into khanates did not immediately end exchange or communication.
The Indian Ocean network depended on monsoon timing and local maritime expertise, not a single technology.
Mali’s wealth came from trade and agriculture; Mansa Musa did not introduce Islam to West Africa for the first time.
A traveler’s account provides situated evidence, not an automatic description of every community.
Crop diffusion can increase food possibilities while disease and land pressure create serious costs.
A comparison needs a shared dimension and reasoning, not three disconnected facts.
The networks overlapped. Do not treat them as sealed compartments.
Do not use later Portuguese expansion or the Columbian Exchange as causes of developments inside 1200–1450.
Avoid unsupported precise epidemic totals, universal claims about regional immunity, or simplistic one-cause explanations.

causalChains.title: Commercial practices → trade
steps: Demand and production created an incentive to move goods.
Caravanserai, credit, and relay exchange reduced some travel or payment problems.
More regular movement strengthened markets and specialized production while leaving costs and risks uneven.

causalChains.title: Trade ↔ state power
steps: States taxed, protected, or redirected routes.
Revenue and information could strengthen political authority.
Rulers still depended on merchants, guides, sailors, farmers, and artisans to make networks work.

causalChains.title: Seasonal travel → diaspora
steps: Monsoon scheduling required waiting, repair, and resupply in ports.
Repeated contact encouraged merchant communities, intermarriage, and shared trust.
Local societies adapted cultural practices in two directions rather than becoming identical.

causalChains.title: Biological exchange → differentiated consequences
steps: Mobility moved crops, animals, people, and pathogens.
Local ecology, institutions, and social power shaped what happened next.
Food possibilities, disease exposure, labor changes, and land pressure varied by region and group.

evidenceGuide.claim: Overland networks depended on nodes and relay exchange.
evidenceGuide.limitation: A city’s importance does not prove it controlled every route.

evidenceGuide.claim: Demand and specialized production reinforced exchange.
evidenceGuide.limitation: Production varied by region and was not modern factory production.

evidenceGuide.claim: Conquest and administration could facilitate some interregional movement.
evidenceGuide.limitation: Security was uneven and built through coercion; routes predated Mongol rule.

evidenceGuide.claim: Knowledge transfer involved adoption and adaptation.
evidenceGuide.limitation: Diffusion does not prove a single society invented every related practice.

evidenceGuide.claim: Monsoon knowledge and technology made seasonal exchange more predictable.
evidenceGuide.limitation: Wind patterns varied by location; no single arrow describes the whole ocean.

evidenceGuide.whereWhen: Kilwa, Mombasa, Calicut, and Malacca, c. 1200–1450
evidenceGuide.claim: Ports connected maritime commerce to interior production and diaspora life.
evidenceGuide.limitation: No one port or empire ruled the entire ocean.

evidenceGuide.claim: Camel logistics and oasis knowledge made desert exchange possible.
evidenceGuide.limitation: Caravans still faced water, security, and political constraints.

evidenceGuide.claim: Trade revenue and patronage connected state power to Islamic scholarship.
evidenceGuide.limitation: Mansa Musa did not introduce Islam to West Africa for the first time.

evidenceGuide.claim: Accounts can reveal encounters, priorities, and judgments.
evidenceGuide.limitation: A traveler is not representative of every community and may be mediated by scribes or translators.

evidenceGuide.claim: Connectivity moved ideas through people and institutions.
evidenceGuide.limitation: Diffusion often produced local adaptation rather than uniform conversion.

evidenceGuide.whereWhen: Champa rice, bananas, and citrus, c. 1200–1450

evidenceGuide.limitation: Crop effects depended on ecology, farming practice, labor, and institutions.

evidenceGuide.claim: Mobility created pathways for pathogens and differentiated demographic effects.
evidenceGuide.limitation: Exact origins, routes, and regional totals require careful corroboration.

guide.unit1Bridge: Unit 1 supplies the agricultural, commercial, religious, political, and scholarly foundations that Unit 2 networks intensified. The chronology overlaps: Unit 2 is not a wholly separate world that begins after Unit 1 ends.
guide.laterCallout: Looking ahead: later European maritime expansion after 1450 changed the scale and power of oceanic exchange. It is a later contrast, not evidence for causes inside this unit.

dimensions.geography: Connected routes through Central Asia, deserts, mountain passes, river valleys, and cities; the category is a network rather than one road.
dimensions.transportEnvironment: Caravans, camel saddles, relay exchange, oasis services, and local route knowledge made difficult land travel possible.
dimensions.representativeGoods: Silk, porcelain, textiles, paper, horses, spices, and other high-value or regionally specialized goods.
dimensions.commercialPractices: Caravanserai, credit, bills of exchange, and currency reduced some carrying, timing, and transaction problems.
dimensions.stateInvolvement: States protected, taxed, administered, or redirected routes unevenly; no single empire controlled the whole network throughout the period.
dimensions.tradingCities: Kashgar, Samarkand, and other nodes supplied water, markets, crafts, information, and cultural institutions.
dimensions.culturalConsequences: Religions, technologies, scientific knowledge, languages, and urban practices moved through merchants, scholars, and officials.
dimensions.environmentalConsequences: Crops, animals, pathogens, and intensified movement altered societies in varied ways; risks and benefits were uneven.

dimensions.geography: Seasonal sea routes linked East Africa, Arabia, Persia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and China through coastal and island ports.
dimensions.transportEnvironment: Sailors combined monsoon timing, local currents, ship design, sails, rudders, compasses, astrolabes, and pilot expertise.
dimensions.representativeGoods: Cotton textiles, pepper, spices, porcelain, silk, gold, ivory, and other products from coastal and interior regions.
dimensions.commercialPractices: Port markets, merchant partnerships, credit, customs, and diaspora trust supported repeated seasonal voyages.
dimensions.stateInvolvement: Swahili cities, Gujarat, Malacca, and other states gained revenue and influence through ports, protection, and strategic passages.
dimensions.tradingCities: Kilwa, Mombasa, Hormuz, Calicut, Malacca, and Hangzhou connected maritime exchange to interior production and consumption.
dimensions.culturalConsequences: Diasporas, intermarriage, Islam, languages, and material culture developed through two-way contact and local adaptation.
dimensions.environmentalConsequences: Crops, disease exposure, coastal settlement, and resource demand moved through routes whose local effects varied.

dimensions.geography: Desert crossings linked North African markets, oasis settlements, Sahel communities, and West African cities.
dimensions.transportEnvironment: Camels, load-bearing saddles, caravans, guides, water planning, oasis stops, and security knowledge structured movement.
dimensions.representativeGoods: Gold, salt, textiles, horses, books, ivory, and other goods moved through multiple intermediaries; people were also subjected to coercive trafficking.
dimensions.commercialPractices: Relay exchange, brokerage, taxation, credit, and market services connected desert logistics to regional production.
dimensions.stateInvolvement: Mali and other states used taxation, protection, political expansion, and patronage to shape exchange while relying on communities and specialists.
dimensions.tradingCities: Taghaza, Walata, Timbuktu, Gao, and a verified North African endpoint connected resources, scholarship, and markets.
dimensions.culturalConsequences: Islamic learning, pilgrimage, scholarship, languages, and local traditions interacted without producing uniform conversion or culture.
dimensions.environmentalConsequences: Desert logistics and biological movement shaped where exchange could occur; water, animals, and land use remained limiting conditions.

places.name: Tunis

seasonalExamples.label: Calicut to Malacca
seasonalExamples.outwardSeason: Use the favorable monsoon season for an eastward voyage; exact departure timing varied by local winds and route.
seasonalExamples.returnSeason: Wait for the seasonal reversal before planning the return westward.
seasonalExamples.feedback: The key historical point is scheduling around seasonal winds and using port communities for waiting, repair, supplies, and exchange. Do not treat one local wind pattern as universal across the ocean.

saharaPlans.label: Plan around water and intermediaries
saharaPlans.choice: Use known oasis stops, a guide with local route expertise, and a cargo plan that leaves capacity for water and supplies.
saharaPlans.feedback: This plan fits desert logistics: water, animals, guides, and security are constraints. It does not guarantee safety or remove unequal power.

saharaPlans.label: Maximize cargo and improvise stops
saharaPlans.choice: Carry as much cargo as possible and assume every settlement can supply water and protection.
saharaPlans.feedback: This plan ignores the environmental and political limits that made oasis knowledge, intermediaries, and caravan organization essential.

activities.title: Trade growth: choose the evidence
activities.claim: Commercial institutions helped turn demand into more regular long-distance exchange.

options.text: Caravanserai and credit reduced some travel or payment problems.
options.feedback: This evidence directly supports the claim because it names an institution and explains its mechanism.

options.text: A ruler was famous in a later period.
options.feedback: This may be historically interesting, but it does not directly show how commercial institutions changed exchange.

options.text: A luxury good was attractive to wealthy consumers.
options.feedback: Demand helps explain growth, but by itself it does not support the specific institutional part of the claim.

activities.title: State power: choose the evidence
activities.claim: States could gain revenue from exchange while relying on specialists and communities to make routes work.

options.text: Mali used taxation and protection while merchants, guides, and producers supplied practical expertise.
options.feedback: This evidence supports both halves of the claim and distinguishes state policy from everyday work.

options.text: A city had a large population in an unspecified century.
options.feedback: A population claim without a period, place, or mechanism does not directly support the relationship.

options.text: All routes were controlled by one empire.
options.feedback: This contradicts the varied and overlapping political arrangements in the unit.

activities.title: Diaspora: choose the evidence
activities.claim: Port communities made seasonal exchange durable by building trust and adapting local practices.

options.text: Merchant communities settled in port cities, intermarried, and used shared commercial relationships.
options.feedback: This evidence names people and mechanisms that connect repeated voyages to durable community life.

options.text: Monsoon winds changed direction each season.
options.feedback: That supports the environmental condition for travel, but not the claim about community formation.

options.text: A state collected a tax from a port.
options.feedback: Taxation can support state power, but it does not by itself show diaspora trust or adaptation.

activities.title: Cultural transfer: choose the evidence
activities.claim: Connectivity moved knowledge through intermediaries, and receiving communities adapted what they received.

options.text: Translators, scholars, merchants, and officials carried and modified paper, medical, or mathematical knowledge.
options.feedback: The evidence identifies carriers and the adaptation mechanism rather than treating diffusion as a one-way gift.
Earlier origins matter, but this fact alone does not show how knowledge moved or changed after 1200.

options.text: A ruler adopted a religion and every subject followed.
options.feedback: The claim requires local agency and variation; universal conversion is unsupported.

activities.title: Environmental consequences: choose the evidence
activities.claim: Connectivity could expand food possibilities and disease exposure at the same time.

options.text: Crop movement supported food production in some settings while mobility created pathways for pathogens.
options.feedback: This evidence supports both sides and leaves room for different local outcomes.

options.text: A trade route crossed a mountain pass.
options.feedback: A route description does not directly show a biological or agricultural consequence.

options.text: Every region experienced exactly the same epidemic loss.
options.feedback: The unit emphasizes uneven evidence and regional variation rather than identical outcomes.

activities.title: Comparison: choose the evidence
activities.claim: The three networks shared broad pressures but solved geographic problems differently.

options.text: Demand and institutions mattered across networks, while monsoon timing, camel logistics, and overland relay produced different solutions.
options.feedback: This evidence makes a comparative claim and explains why the difference existed.
This is true but too general to show a meaningful similarity or difference.

options.text: One network was simply better than the others.
options.feedback: A historical comparison needs criteria and reasoning rather than an unsupported ranking.

topics.title: Cultural Consequences of Connectivity
topics.summary: How trade and travel moved religions, scientific knowledge, technologies, and perspectives while producing local adaptation.
topics.bigIdea: Connectivity spread ideas through movement, but recipients adapted, combined, resisted, or reinterpreted what they encountered.

topics.title: Environmental Consequences of Connectivity
topics.summary: How connected exchange changed crops, populations, disease patterns, labor, and land use across Afro-Eurasia.
topics.bigIdea: Exchange could support food production and population growth while also spreading disease and increasing pressure on land; outcomes depended on local conditions and choices.

topics.title: Comparison of Economic Exchange
topics.summary: A method for comparing the Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan networks with specific evidence and explained reasoning.
topics.bigIdea: All three networks connected producers and consumers and depended on political and environmental conditions, but their routes, technologies, goods, and state structures produced meaningful differences.
